spec_match.rationale: Demonstrates the motivating contract of the feature — gradient interpolation happens in the canvas backing store's colour space — using identical drawing code against srgb and srgb-linear stores and sampling midpoints via getImageData({ colorSpace: 'srgb' }) so the comparison is apples-to-apples.

interactive.rationale: Two colour pickers and a redraw button drive both panels; midpoint chips and byte readouts update live, and the summed-linear-light comparison recomputes per draw.

blurb_alignment.rationale: The card promises side-by-side interpolation domains with a sampled midpoint, which the page delivers with numbers.

edge_cases.rationale: When the linear store is rejected the lower panel switches to a JS reference rendering that is triple-labelled (banner, amber panel badge, readout suffix) as a simulation; the explanation also covers stop pairs where the two domains nearly agree.

references.rationale: Links chromestatus.com/feature/5122501071994880, CSS Color 4 srgb-linear, and sibling concepts.

conformance.rationale: The suite's linear-gradient-midpoint-preserves-light assertion encodes this page's exact claim (linear midpoint brighter than gamma midpoint by a numeric bound, sampled as srgb bytes); verified executing on the /conformance/ route.

runtime_evidence.rationale: Headless Chromium 141 (chrome-devtools-mcp unavailable here): autorun DOM shows gamma midpoint [127,0,127] vs linear [187,0,188]; desktop screenshot read and shows the muddy-vs-bright middle plus the amber simulation badge; mobile 360 clean with no page overflow; zero page console errors over CDP.

telemetry_health.rationale: Asserts gradient-native-linear-store or gradient-js-reference-fallback on load and gradient-midpoints-sampled per redraw with the sampled bytes as details.

design_system.rationale: Chrome colours are styles.css variables; the native/reference badges use accent-emerald/accent-amber on light-on-dark pairs that pass AA; buttons set background and color together.

accessibility.rationale: Colour inputs are labelled, canvases carry role=img with aria-labels naming the interpolation domain, midpoint readouts are aria-live text (not colour-only — bytes are printed), and focus-visible outlines are explicit.

mobile_desktop_parity.rationale: Canvases scale to 100% width; CDP-measured scrollWidth equals innerWidth at 360x740 DPR3; both class screenshots read.

openQuestions.title: Capture native srgb-linear gradient evidence on a Chrome 155 build
openQuestions.detail: On Chromium 141 the lower panel necessarily runs the labelled JS reference rendering. On a 155/flag-enabled browser, verify the native panel's badge flips to 'native canvas', the midpoint bytes match the reference math within rounding, and the conformance assertion linear-gradient-midpoint-preserves-light passes.

guidanceConsulted.query: wide gamut display-p3 CSS color feature detection fallback
guidanceConsulted.recommendation: modern-web-guidance returned no gradient-banding-specific guide; nearest results (dark-mode, css) stress honest capability handling and token-driven colour.
guidanceConsulted.appliedOrException: Exception recorded: no direct guide exists for canvas colour-space comparisons. Applied the general principles — exact-surface feature detection with readback, clearly-labelled non-native fallback, and design-token chrome around raw demo-content colours (the raw colours ARE the feature under demonstration).

guidanceConsulted.recommendation: Visual-only output needs a text equivalent; announce state changes via live regions.
guidanceConsulted.appliedOrException: Every visual comparison is mirrored by printed midpoint bytes and a summed-luminance sentence in aria-live regions; canvases have role=img aria-labels.

summary: The practical why-this-matters concept: identical gradient code against gamma and linear stores with sampled midpoints proving the muddy-middle artefact. Falls back to a triple-labelled JS reference rendering where the linear store is rejected. Verified in headless Chromium 141, both device classes, clean console.
